newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Browsing in range as silver perks up.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Browsing in range as silver perks up.

text.p: The gold price may see some slippage this week but is unlikely to drop out of its range, especially after silver's small recovery last Friday, analysts said.
"People may get a little bit nervous if it hangs around too long," said Tony Warwick-Ching, precious metals consultant at CRU International.
"Having said that, I don't think it's going to be pushed out the way. There isn't a strong case for it," he added.
Gold was at the whim of a falling silver market last week as funds, disenchanted by silver's lack of follow-through above $5.30 per ounce after an earlier rally this year, liquidated positions.
But silver clawed back to $4.78 in overnight dealings on Friday with Comex futures contracts finishing slightly higher.
Bullion clung to support at $347.00 an ounce, staying clear of $345.00 which chart analysts said if breached might trigger a raid on $340.00 before physical offtake came into play.

But upside potential was also capped by concerns of fresh U.S. interest rate hikes as the economy continued to show signs of heating up, and the Federal Reserve (central bank) remained anxious to keep inflation in check.
Dealers will continue to focus on U.S. economic data this week to gauge when the Fed is likely to raise interest rates again.
"There is a little bit of uneasy feeling at the moment that there may be more (rises) on the way as the summer progresses," said Warwick-Ching.
Key fundamental data is due on Friday when the March producer price index and retail sales figures will be released.
Meanwhile gold was unlikely to benefit greatly from an influx of hot money from tumbling stocks or bonds, dealers said, and it remained beset by fears of renewed central bank sales.
"Unfortunately gold is not the first port of call it used to be when other financial markets are in trouble," said Warwick-Ching.
Comex May options expire on Friday but dealers expected little activity in gold with the main interest being in silver options.
Silver took a battering last week, losing 40 cents to end at $4.72/$4.74, but dealers suggested that fund liquidation seemed to be drying up and recovery could continue this week.
"It does look overdone but that doesn't mean they (the funds) can't come and have another go," he said.
However, CPM Group New York analyst Ted Kempf said silver was unlikely to linger at these low levels for much longer given the strong demand for physical material from fabricators.
Support is expected to come in solidly at Thursday's low of $4.65, but an assault to $4.50 may scare investors.
Gold will be looking to hold above $346.50, from where it bounced up on Friday.

Negative sentiment also affected platinum and palladium last week but dealers noted underlying support while there were no talks between Russia and Japan on PGM sale contracts which expired at the end of 1996.

The trade representative of the Russian Federation in Japan, Y.F. Zhigulov, said on Monday there would be no shipments to Japan in April and that May shipments were in doubt. He said Almaz, Russia's platinum group metal export agency, had not yet received its export licence.
"While that's still unresolved I can't see it pushing too far down," said one.

To some extent, PGMs fortunes will also depend on silver this week. Platinum ended last Friday $3.00 lower at $362.50/$363.50, while palladium bucked the trend and closed slightly higher. -- Clelia Oziel +44-171-542 8072
